speaker: periodista
text: Good afternoon and welcome to our press conference with President Lagarde and Vice President de Guindos.

speaker: periodista
text: My name is Wolfgang Preusel. As always, we have some participants who are connected via video.

speaker: periodista
text: When they take the floor, I would ask them to turn on the camera and their microphones.

speaker: periodista
text: And with that, I would like to hand over to President Lagarde, please.

speaker: presidenta
text: Thank you very much and good day to all of you.

speaker: presidenta
text: The Vice President and I welcome you to our press conference.

speaker: presidenta
text: The Governing Council today decided to keep the three key ECB interest rates unchanged.

speaker: presidenta
text: We are determined to ensure that inflation stabilizes at our 2% target in the medium term.

speaker: presidenta
text: The war in the Middle East has made the outlook significantly more uncertain,

speaker: presidenta
text: creating upside risks for inflation and downside risks for economic growth.

speaker: presidenta
text: It will have a material impact on near-term inflation through higher energy prices.

speaker: presidenta
text: Its medium-term implications will depend both on the intensity and duration of the conflict,

speaker: presidenta
text: and how the energy prices affect consumer prices in the economy.

speaker: presidenta
text: We are well positioned to navigate this uncertainty.

speaker: presidenta
text: Inflation has been at around 2% target,

speaker: presidenta
text: longer-term inflation expectations are well anchored,

speaker: presidenta
text: and the economy has shown resilience over recent quarters.

speaker: presidenta
text: The incoming information in the period ahead

speaker: presidenta
text: will help us assess how the war will affect the inflation outlook

speaker: presidenta
text: and the risks surrounding it.

speaker: presidenta
text: We are closely monitoring the situation, and our data-dependent approach will help us set monetary policy as appropriate.

speaker: presidenta
text: The new ECB staff projections exceptionally incorporate information up to the 11th of March, a later cut-off date than usual. In the baseline, headline inflation is seen to average 2.6% in 2026, 2% in 2027, and 2.1% in 2028.

speaker: presidenta
text: Inflation has been revised up compared with the December projections, especially for 26.

speaker: presidenta
text: And this is because energy prices will be higher owing to the war in the Middle East.

speaker: presidenta
text: For inflation excluding energy and food, staff project an average of 2.3% in 2016, 2.2% in 2017 and 2.1% in 2018.

speaker: presidenta
text: This is also higher than the path in the December projections, mainly owing to higher energy prices feeding into inflation excluding energy and food.

speaker: presidenta
text: Staff expect economic growth to average 0.9% in 2016, 1.3% in 2017, and 1.4% in 2018.

speaker: presidenta
text: This implies a downward revision, especially for 2016, reflecting the global effects of

speaker: presidenta
text: the war on commodity markets, real incomes, and confidence.

speaker: presidenta
text: At the same time, low unemployment, solid private sector balance sheets, and public spending

speaker: presidenta
text: on defence and infrastructure should continue to underpin growth.

speaker: presidenta
text: In line with our monetary policy strategy commitment to incorporate risks and uncertainty

speaker: presidenta
text: into our decision-making, staff also assessed how the war in the Middle East could affect

speaker: presidenta
text: economic growth and inflation under some alternative illustrative scenarios.

speaker: presidenta
text: These scenarios will be published with the staff projections on our website.

speaker: presidenta
text: The scenario analysis suggests that a prolonged disruption in the supply of oil and gas would

speaker: presidenta
text: result in inflation being above and growth being below the baseline projection.

speaker: presidenta
text: The implications for medium-term inflation depend crucially on the magnitude of indirect

speaker: presidenta
text: and second-round effects of a stronger and more persistent energy shock.

speaker: presidenta
text: We will follow a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach to determining the appropriate monetary

speaker: presidenta
text: policy stance.

speaker: presidenta
text: In particular, our interest rate decisions will be based on our assessment of the inflation

speaker: presidenta
text: outlook and the risks surrounding it in light of the incoming economic and financial data,

speaker: presidenta
text: as well as the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy transmission.

speaker: presidenta
text: We are not pre-committing to a particular rate path.

speaker: presidenta
text: The decisions taken today are set out in a press release available on our website.

speaker: presidenta
text: So I will now outline in more detail how we see the economy and inflation developing,

speaker: presidenta
text: and will then explain our assessment of financial and monetary conditions.

speaker: presidenta
text: Looking at the economic activity, the economy grew by 0.2 percent in the fourth quarter

speaker: presidenta
text: of 2025, driven by stronger domestic demand.

speaker: presidenta
text: Exports increased their spending as real income rose, and unemployment remained close to its

speaker: presidenta
text: historical low.

speaker: presidenta
text: Construction and housing renovation strengthened, and firms invested more, particularly in areas

speaker: presidenta
text: such as research and development, software and databases.

speaker: presidenta
text: Growth was no longer weighed down by net exports as it had been in the previous two quarters.

speaker: presidenta
text: It was underpinned mainly by services.

speaker: presidenta
text: Staff still see private consumption as the main driver of growth over the medium term.

speaker: presidenta
text: Investment should also continue to grow, with government spending more on defence and on

speaker: presidenta
text: infrastructure, and firms increasingly investing in new digital technologies.

speaker: presidenta
text: The external environment remains challenging, including in light of volatile global trade

speaker: presidenta
text: policies.

speaker: presidenta
text: The war in the Middle East is disrupting commodity markets and weighing on real incomes and confidence.

speaker: presidenta
text: This has led to a downward revision of consumption and investment in the baseline staff projections,

speaker: presidenta
text: especially for 2026.

speaker: presidenta
text: The impact would be even more pronounced in alternative scenarios, with a more severe

speaker: presidenta
text: and prolonged energy shock.

speaker: presidenta
text: The Governing Council highlights the urgent need to strengthen the euro-area economy while

speaker: presidenta
text: maintaining sound public finances.

speaker: presidenta
text: Any fiscal responses to the energy price shock should be temporary, targeted and tailored.

speaker: presidenta
text: The current energy crisis underscores the imperative to further reduce dependence on

speaker: presidenta
text: fossil fuels.

speaker: presidenta
text: Completing the Savings and Investments Union is vital to fund innovation and support the

speaker: presidenta
text: green and digital transitions.

speaker: presidenta
text: The digital euro and tokenized wholesale central bank money will enhance Europe's strategic

speaker: presidenta
text: autonomy, competitiveness and financial integration, and will boost innovation in payments.

speaker: presidenta
text: It is thus essential to swiftly adopt the regulation on the establishment of the digital euro.

speaker: presidenta
text: Simplifying and harmonizing rules across the EU single market will help European firms

speaker: presidenta
text: grow faster.

speaker: presidenta
text: Looking now at inflation.

speaker: presidenta
text: Inflation rose to 1.9 percent in February from 1.7 percent in January.

speaker: presidenta
text: Energy prices were 3.1 percent lower than a year ago after having been 4 percent lower

speaker: presidenta
text: in January.

speaker: presidenta
text: Food price inflation edged down to 2.5%.

speaker: presidenta
text: Inflation excluding energy and food increased to 2.4% in February from 2.2% in January.

speaker: presidenta
text: The increase reflected goods inflation rising to 0.7% from 0.4% and services inflation moving

speaker: presidenta
text: up to 3.4 percent from 3.2 percent.

speaker: presidenta
text: Indicators of underlying inflation have changed little over recent months and remain consistent

speaker: presidenta
text: with our 2 percent medium-term target.

speaker: presidenta
text: Corporate profits recovered further in the fourth quarter of 2025, while unit labour

speaker: presidenta
text: costs rose at a similar rate as in the previous quarter.

speaker: presidenta
text: Growth in compensation per employee slowed to 3.7% from 4% in the third quarter.

speaker: presidenta
text: Negotiated wage growth and forward-looking indicators such as the ECB wage tracker and

speaker: presidenta
text: surveys on wage expectations suggest that labour costs will ease further in the course

speaker: presidenta
text: of 2026, which should support the return of inflation to target.

speaker: presidenta
text: The increase in energy prices caused by the war will drive inflation above 2% in the near

speaker: presidenta
text: term.

speaker: presidenta
text: If persistent higher energy prices may lead to a broader increase in inflation through

speaker: presidenta
text: indirect and second round effects, a situation which requires close monitoring, inflation

speaker: presidenta
text: Inflation expectations in the financial markets have moved up significantly over shorter horizons.

speaker: presidenta
text: Most measures of longer-term inflation expectations stand at around 2%, supporting the stabilization

speaker: presidenta
text: of inflation around our target.

speaker: presidenta
text: Let us now turn to our risk assessment.

speaker: presidenta
text: The risks to the growth outlook are tilted to the downside, especially in the near term.

speaker: presidenta
text: The war in the Middle East is a downside risk to the euro-area economy, adding to the volatile

speaker: presidenta
text: global policy environment.

speaker: presidenta
text: A prolonged war could increase energy prices further and for longer than currently expected,

speaker: presidenta
text: and also weigh on confidence.

speaker: presidenta
text: These factors would erode incomes and make firms and households more reluctant to invest

speaker: presidenta
text: and spend.

speaker: presidenta
text: A worsening of global financial market sentiment could further dampen demand.

speaker: presidenta
text: Additional frictions in international trade could disrupt supply chains, reduce exports

speaker: presidenta
text: and weaken consumption and investment.

speaker: presidenta
text: Other geopolitical tensions, in particular Russia's unjustified war against Ukraine,

speaker: presidenta
text: remain a major source of uncertainty.

speaker: presidenta
text: By contrast, growth could turn out to be higher if the economic repercussions of the war in

speaker: presidenta
text: the Middle East proved to be more short-lived than currently expected.

speaker: presidenta
text: In addition, planned defence and infrastructure spending, reforms to enhance productivity,

speaker: presidenta
text: and euro-area firms adopting new technologies may drive up growth by more than expected.

speaker: presidenta
text: New trade agreements and a deeper integration of the single market could also boost growth

speaker: presidenta
text: beyond current expectations.

speaker: presidenta
text: The risks to the inflation outlook are tilted to the upside, especially in the near term.

speaker: presidenta
text: A prolonged war in the Middle East could lead to a larger and longer-lasting upward shift

speaker: presidenta
text: in energy prices than currently expected, raising euro area inflation further.

speaker: presidenta
text: This could be reinforced and become more persistent if inflation expectations and wage growth

speaker: presidenta
text: growth were to rise in response, if the energy price increase were to spill over to non-energy

speaker: presidenta
text: inflation to a larger extent than assumed in the baseline, or if the war disrupted global

speaker: presidenta
text: supply chains more broadly.

speaker: presidenta
text: Ongoing trade tensions could also give rise to more fragmented global supply chains, curtail

speaker: presidenta
text: the supply of critical raw materials and tighten capacity constraints in the euro-area economy.

speaker: presidenta
text: By contrast, inflation could turn out to be lower if the economic repercussions of the

speaker: presidenta
text: war in the Middle East proved to be more short-lived or if indirect and second-round effects proved

speaker: presidenta
text: less pronounced than currently expected.

speaker: presidenta
text: Inflation could also be lower if tariffs reduced demand for Euro-area exports by more than

speaker: presidenta
text: expected and if countries with overcapacity increased further their exports to the Euro-area.

speaker: presidenta
text: More volatile and risk-averse financial markets could weigh on demand and thereby lower inflation

speaker: presidenta
text: as well.

speaker: presidenta
text: So looking at the financial and monetary conditions, the war in the Middle East has had a pronounced

speaker: presidenta
text: impact on global financial markets.

speaker: presidenta
text: Overall, financial conditions have tightened since our last meeting.

speaker: presidenta
text: Stock markets have fallen, and market interest rates in the euro area, especially short-term

speaker: presidenta
text: rates, have risen notably.

speaker: presidenta
text: In January, bank lending rates for firms and the cost of issuing market-based debt both

speaker: presidenta
text: remained at 3.6%, while the average interest rate on new mortgages edged up to 3.4%.

speaker: presidenta
text: Bank lending to firms grew by 2.8% on a yearly basis in January, down from 3% in December.

speaker: presidenta
text: However, this was offset by stronger issuance of corporate bonds, with the annual growth

speaker: presidenta
text: rate rising to 4 percent from 3.5 percent in December.

speaker: presidenta
text: Mortgage lending grew by 3 percent and changed from December.

speaker: presidenta
text: So in conclusion, the Governing Council today decided to keep the three key ECB interest

speaker: presidenta
text: rates unchanged.

speaker: presidenta
text: We are determined to ensure that inflation stabilizes at our 2 percent target in the

speaker: presidenta
text: medium term.

speaker: presidenta
text: We will follow a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach to determining the appropriate monetary

speaker: presidenta
text: policy stance.

speaker: presidenta
text: Our interest rate decisions will be based on our assessment of the inflation outlook

speaker: presidenta
text: and the risks surrounding it, in light of the incoming economic and financial data,

speaker: presidenta
text: as well as the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy transmission.

speaker: presidenta
text: We are not pre-committing to a particular rate path.

speaker: presidenta
text: In any case, we stand ready to adjust all of our instruments within our mandate to

speaker: presidenta
text: ensure that inflation stabilizes sustainably at our medium-term target and to preserve

speaker: presidenta
text: the smooth functioning of monetary policy transmission.

speaker: presidenta
text: And we are now ready to take your questions.

speaker: periodista
text: And the first question goes to Annette Weisbach of CNBC, Annette, please.

speaker: vicepresidente
text: Thank you very much.

speaker: vicepresidente
text: President Lagarde, I have two questions, obviously.

speaker: vicepresidente
text: So the first one is how the discussion went inside the governing council regarding the

speaker: vicepresidente
text: very uncertain outlook for monetary policy, whether you are all in one camp or whether

speaker: vicepresidente
text: there is perhaps a range of opinions. Second question is on the markets, because the markets

speaker: vicepresidente
text: are trying to understand how fast you're willing to act. You work quite fast in the projections

speaker: vicepresidente
text: already reflecting the changed situation, I would say. So is it the next meeting perhaps

speaker: vicepresidente
text: we're going to see action? And when is the medium, when the medium term obviously is

speaker: vicepresidente
text: a longer term, but when do you think it is time to act? Thank you.

speaker: presidenta
text: Thank you very much for your two questions.

speaker: presidenta
text: Let me give you a little bit of the ambiance and the process through which we went in the

speaker: presidenta
text: last couple of days.

speaker: presidenta
text: We had an in-depth discussion on the current situation, and we are ever so grateful that

speaker: presidenta
text: our staff, at the risk of having zero weekends and very, very short nights, was able to provide

speaker: presidenta
text: us with a baseline and scenarios, the overall projection efforts, as at March the 11th.

speaker: presidenta
text: This is very unusual, and I'm specifically included in the monetary policy statement

speaker: presidenta
text: that this is exceptional.

speaker: presidenta
text: I don't wish to impose that exercise on a regular basis,

speaker: presidenta
text: but this was the information

speaker: presidenta
text: from which we could actually discuss in depth.

speaker: presidenta
text: We went a bit further than that,

speaker: presidenta
text: and we managed to make sure

speaker: presidenta
text: that the members of the Governing Council

speaker: presidenta
text: were extensively briefed by experts.

speaker: presidenta
text: We had a defense and military affairs professor

speaker: presidenta
text: who briefed us the day before the governing council meeting.

speaker: presidenta
text: And by, you know, the randomness of calendar scheduling,

speaker: presidenta
text: we also had a very good presentation

speaker: presidenta
text: of climate change impact on the ocean.

speaker: presidenta
text: And it's not unrelated in many ways.

speaker: presidenta
text: But it's totally random, I can assure you.

speaker: presidenta
text: So I think my goal and the goal of the executive board

speaker: presidenta
text: was to make sure that governors were starting

speaker: presidenta
text: from the best-informed basis to hold their in-depth discussion.

speaker: presidenta
text: And I would characterize the overall mood of the group

speaker: presidenta
text: as being calm, being determined, and being laser-focused

speaker: presidenta
text: on the information that we have, the projections

speaker: presidenta
text: that we received, and all data that can be analyzed

speaker: presidenta
text: and factored into our decision-making process.

speaker: presidenta
text: Our decision was unanimous.

speaker: presidenta
text: So you asked me about a range of views.

speaker: presidenta
text: There was no range of views.

speaker: presidenta
text: It was a unanimous decision that was taken,

speaker: presidenta
text: not to move rates at all.

speaker: presidenta
text: We are going to continue doing what we have been doing.

speaker: presidenta
text: And that's addressing the second part of your question.

speaker: presidenta
text: You know, we are starting from a good base.

speaker: presidenta
text: So I'm not saying that we are in a good place.

speaker: presidenta
text: We are well-positioned.

speaker: presidenta
text: And actually, you find that in the monetary policy statement.

speaker: presidenta
text: I think we are both well-positioned and well-equipped

speaker: presidenta
text: to deal with the development of a major shock

speaker: presidenta
text: that is unfolding, and we will continue doing that.

speaker: presidenta
text: You probably have heard me ad nauseum say,

speaker: presidenta
text: meeting by meeting, data dependent, no preset pace.

speaker: presidenta
text: And this was embedded in our strategy review of last July.

speaker: presidenta
text: But I'm so pleased that we finalized our agreement

speaker: presidenta
text: to operate on that basis, which is proving extremely helpful

speaker: presidenta
text: Because at the time, we anticipated that we would be facing a succession of shocks, possibly in closed sequence.

speaker: presidenta
text: And this is what we are seeing at the moment.

speaker: presidenta
text: That's what we will do, which explains that I cannot give you a timeline, a date, but I can assure you that we will proceed on the basis of this analysis,

speaker: presidenta
text: And on the basis of the hard work produced by staff to make sure that we have not only the baseline that you will see after this press conference, because it will be published, but also the scenarios that you will also see after the press conference, because it will also be on the website. Thank you.

speaker: periodista
text: Next question is for Balazs Korani of Reuters. Balazs, please.
good afternoon thanks for taking my questions first one is about your reaction function if you could explain that a little bit what would trigger ECB action are you looking at expectations
are you looking at core inflation is it wage growth that needs to move what is it that you're
that would get the ECB to actually act the second is could you please preview the alternative
scenarios for us.
I'm curious about the adverse scenario.
What does it look like?
How high inflation goes?
How long would it take to fall back?
And how much of the energy shock would translate
into core inflation?
Yeah.

speaker: presidenta
text: OK.

speaker: presidenta
text: OK.

speaker: presidenta
text: Well, I hope everybody else will be patient,

speaker: presidenta
text: because I might take a little longer than I normally take.

speaker: presidenta
text: But I hope it informs all of you.

speaker: presidenta
text: So, as I said, we will continue to apply the three key principles that I have outlined.

speaker: presidenta
text: And being data dependent will lead us to look at everything that we normally look at.

speaker: presidenta
text: But we will be particularly attentive to a number of things.

speaker: presidenta
text: And that's, I think, the point in your question.

speaker: presidenta
text: We will be particularly attentive to developments in all commodity markets.

speaker: presidenta
text: We will be particularly attentive to supply bottlenecks.

speaker: presidenta
text: We will be particularly attentive to selling price expectations of firms.

speaker: presidenta
text: And, you know, through the corporate telephone survey in particular and other surveys that we hold of good value,

speaker: presidenta
text: we can assess how often price revisions will take place.

speaker: presidenta
text: That will be important.

speaker: presidenta
text: We will be particularly attentive to all demand indicators,

speaker: presidenta
text: you know, be it PMIs, consumer confidence, et cetera.

speaker: presidenta
text: We will be particularly attentive to wage trackers.

speaker: presidenta
text: Because what we want to really come back to is these three key points

speaker: presidenta
text: that I have mentioned and that are also in the monetary policy statement.

speaker: presidenta
text: All of that which is unfolding at the moment, which is a severe shock,

speaker: presidenta
text: will depend on the duration, the intensity, and the propagation.

speaker: presidenta
text: And by propagation, I mean the indirect effects and the second round effects.

speaker: presidenta
text: And we need to have the best sensors and the best way to anticipate

speaker: presidenta
text: where these indirect effects and where these second round effects are going, if at all.

speaker: presidenta
text: That's what we will be attentive to.

speaker: presidenta
text: Now, I'm going to try to take you through a little bit to the scenarios,

speaker: presidenta
text: but I very strongly encourage you to look at the material

speaker: presidenta
text: that we will be releasing after this press conference,

speaker: presidenta
text: which will be far more detailed and informative.

speaker: presidenta
text: But essentially, the work that was done by staff is the following.

speaker: presidenta
text: Number one, they did a first baseline as at March 4th,

speaker: presidenta
text: which would have been normal exercise.

speaker: presidenta
text: And that will be available as well in what we publish later today.

speaker: presidenta
text: But that was very quickly superseded by the turn of events.

speaker: presidenta
text: So they did a second baseline as at March 11th.

speaker: presidenta
text: And that is the baseline that we hold as our baseline in our projections.

speaker: presidenta
text: And you will find all the hypotheticals that are used there in terms of the price of oil, the price of gas,

speaker: presidenta
text: and the duration of the shock and the propagation.

speaker: presidenta
text: And there is a bit of propagation, actually, some of it being judgmental, you know, some indirect effects, some secondary effects as well.

speaker: presidenta
text: And then they produced two scenarios.

speaker: presidenta
text: One is the adverse scenario, and the other one is the severe scenario.

speaker: presidenta
text: Now, you will ask me, you know, what's the difference between the two?

speaker: presidenta
text: In the severe scenario, the price of oil and gas goes significantly up and higher than in the baseline,

speaker: presidenta
text: but it falls back to March 4th baseline, pretty much at the end of our projection horizon.

speaker: presidenta
text: On the other hand, the severe one, it goes up as well, a little higher than in the adverse, But it doesn't fall back very fast, so it stays high for a longer period of time, and it settles at March 4th baseline beyond the end of our projection horizon.

speaker: presidenta
text: That's one of the key differences, and obviously, given the hypotheses that are taken, the impact on inflation, on growth, are different and are higher on inflation and lower on growth.

speaker: presidenta
text: But I'm not going to give you the year-by-year details of those consequences. You will find that in the scenarios, but it's a significant difference.

speaker: periodista
text: Next question goes to Jana Randor of Bloomberg. Jana, please.
Good afternoon. Two questions. How are the lessons of the 2022 inflation shock informing your approach to the current crisis?
You've said in the run-up to the meeting that you won't allow the same kind of inflation to materialize again.
And so I'm wondering whether your threshold is lower than in the past and potentially also a bit closer.
That will be my first question.
And the second one relates to the core inflation projections.
I noticed that they are above 2 percent, not much, but they are above 2 percent throughout the forecast horizon.
And I'm wondering if those are all ready second round effects.
And more generally, I would be interested in how you feel about those projections in relation to your mandate.

speaker: presidenta
text: Thank you. I feel very proud of our staff, that I can assure you.

speaker: presidenta
text: Because I don't think that there are many other central banks that have had the courage to try to cut off at March 11th

speaker: presidenta
text: and produce the set of data that we have had available.

speaker: presidenta
text: That's how I feel.

speaker: presidenta
text: So, from 2022 to now, four years later, I would characterize our current position as, I would have two characteristics.

speaker: presidenta
text: One is, I think we are well positioned, and I would call it the three times two.

speaker: presidenta
text: 2% inflation at around target medium term, 2% medium term inflation expectations, and 2% interest rates.

speaker: presidenta
text: So target, target, broadly neutral.

speaker: presidenta
text: That leads me to say that we start from a good position,

speaker: presidenta
text: and we are well positioned to demonstrate our capacity to apply our strategy and to be agile,

speaker: presidenta
text: to do what is necessary because, second point,

speaker: presidenta
text: we are determined to ensure

speaker: presidenta
text: that inflation stabilizes

speaker: presidenta
text: at 2% medium term.

speaker: presidenta
text: This is our commitment.

speaker: presidenta
text: When I say also

speaker: presidenta
text: that we are well equipped,

speaker: presidenta
text: I think that, you know,

speaker: presidenta
text: in those four years,

speaker: presidenta
text: we have learned,

speaker: presidenta
text: we have improved our models,

speaker: presidenta
text: we have changed our strategy,

speaker: presidenta
text: And we are now, in particular, more attentive to risks around the outlook.

speaker: presidenta
text: We are developing scenarios, sensitivity analysis to make sure that we are as well informed as possible in order to assess the situation.

speaker: presidenta
text: So I would say that this enables us to better understand and better make our determination.

speaker: presidenta
text: I think we also understand better the mechanism of the pass-through

speaker: presidenta
text: into indirect and second-round effects.

speaker: presidenta
text: So on your second question, as I said,

speaker: presidenta
text: I'm proud of the projections that have been delivered.

speaker: presidenta
text: Granted, on core, we are 2.1 in 2028.

speaker: presidenta
text: You have to remember that we include in that ETS2, applying as of 28, and you still have a little bit of remaining of the base effect and a little bit of second round.

speaker: periodista
text: The next question goes to Elisa Piazza of CNBC, Class CNBC. Elisa, please.

Thank you for taking my questions. Well, my first question is how concerned is the ECB about private credit in the US? So do you see potential contagion risks in the broader financial system, so in Europe as well?

And my second question is about the European Commission that is considering a review of EU merger rules to encourage cross-border consolidation, including in the banking system, while national authorities continue to pose obstacles to such transactions.
So, what's the ECB's view on this?
I'm not making names.

speaker: presidenta
text: Well, thank you for being so discreet about names, but you also give me a chance to offer the floor to my vice president, whom I am so grateful.
Well, good afternoon.
If you look at our recent financial stability reports, we have been dealing with private
credit quite a lot, and we have paid a lot of attention to private credit, and the potential
risks that private credit and private equity, private markets in general, have posed for
financial stability, and while the exposure in Europe of private credit and private markets

This is an indication of all the problems that I have indicated before, that I have seen out before.
And, you know, it's a clear indication that, well, there are liquidity mismatches in this kind of funds.
The interconnection with, you know, the banks and the non-banks is something that we have analyzed quite in detail.
As I have said before, in the case of Europe, it's much more limited exposure to this kind of instruments.
But, well, it's something that we are following closely.
I'm for sure that what is happening in the U.S. could be a sort of leading gator.
Nevertheless, I repeat again that exposure in Europe is much more limited of the European banks to this kind of instruments.

I think that we need much more transparency

And, well, the links and the interconnections with the banks
